crm_note.headline: Mei Lin Tan, second round at Fernhallow Capital done on 2026-11-10: live Python and a backtest review, awaiting feedback
crm_note.how_it_went: The second round ran about two and a quarter hours, with a live Python task followed by a backtest case. Mei Lin felt the Python hour went well, as the interviewer said she cared about the logic rather than exact syntax. She thinks the case went well but was hand-wavy on modelling market impact for small caps.

rounds.format: About an hour with Nadia Osei, a researcher on the equities side. Live Python on a provided laptop with no internet. One probability warm-up question at the start.
asked: Build a simple reversal signal from daily prices and volumes for a few hundred stocks over about ten years, and describe the performance. The data was deliberately messy, with series that end part-way through, gaps and a couple of obviously bad prints.
Probability warm-up: a stick is broken at two random points, what is the chance the three pieces form a triangle.
rounds.candidate_view: Mei Lin said she could not recall exact groupby syntax, so she said she would normally check the docs and wrote pseudo-pandas. Nadia said that was fine as she cared about the logic. Mei Lin raised survivorship bias and asked why some series ended (delisted, acquired) before computing anything, and said Nadia smiled. She answered the probability question with a quarter and said she had seen it before and told them so.

rounds.format: Case with Nadia Osei and a second researcher, Pieter (surname not caught). They showed a backtest with a Sharpe of about 2.1 and asked what was wrong with it.
asked: What is wrong with this backtest?
How many variants did she think had been tried to arrive at this one?
How would she model market impact for small caps, and what participation rate?
rounds.candidate_view: Mei Lin covered look-ahead (close prices used to trade at the same close), costs and the very high turnover, and multiple testing, including deflating the Sharpe for the number of trials. She thinks it landed well. The interviewers pushed on costs more than she expected, and she said she was a bit hand-wavy on small-cap market impact and participation rate.

compensation.notes: Compensation did not come up in the interview. Mei Lin said she is not moving sideways.

crm_note.notice_and_non_compete: Notice is three months and the non-compete is six months, with paid garden leave. Nadia asked about notice and did not react to the answer.
competing_processes: Final round at a large multi-manager (a pod) next week, in the week starting 2026-11-16
risks: Mei Lin is worried the team is small (the PM, Marcus, and a few researchers) and what would happen to her if he left. She has seen this happen to a friend.
Mei Lin was hand-wavy on small-cap market impact and participation rate, and the interviewers pushed on costs.
Her salary expectation is above her current base and she has a final round elsewhere next week.

next_actions.action: Chase Fernhallow for feedback on the second round
Suggest Mei Lin asks Marcus directly at the final about the small team and what happens if he leaves

candidate.subject: Fernhallow second round
candidate.body:
Hi Mei Lin,

Thanks for talking me through the second round so soon afterwards, I hope you got your rest.

To recap the next steps: I will chase Fernhallow for feedback by the end of this week and let you know as soon as I hear anything. As we discussed, if you reach the final, it would be worth asking Marcus directly about the team size question you raised.

In the meantime, let me know if anything else comes to mind from the day.

Best wishes,
Hannah

client.subject: Mei Lin Tan, second round feedback
client.body:
Hi,

I spoke to Mei Lin Tan after her second round for the Quantitative Researcher, Systematic Equities role. She described the day as a live Python task followed by a backtest review case, and she remains interested in the role.

Could you let me know the team's feedback and any next steps when you have them? I will chase you towards the end of this week.

Kind regards,
Hannah

process.format: Video call of about forty-five minutes. Around ten minutes on the CV, then probability questions typed into a shared document. No coding.
process.what_they_look_for: Careful probability reasoning (including checking an answer and explaining why similar problems differ) and rigorous validation of past research, such as out-of-sample testing and who chose the holdout. He gave almost no reaction during the call.

process.format: At the firm's office, a little over two hours (about two and a quarter on the day, after a late start). Hour one was live Python on a company laptop with no internet, plus one probability warm-up question. Hour two was a case where a backtest was shown and the candidate was asked what was wrong with it.
process.who: Nadia Osei, a researcher on the equities side, for both hours. A second researcher, Pieter (surname not caught), joined for the case.
process.what_they_look_for: Sound logic over exact syntax (Nadia said she cared about the logic, and pseudo-code was accepted). Noticing problems in messy data, such as series that end part-way through, and spotting flaws in a backtest, including look-ahead, costs, turnover and multiple testing.

process.format: About three hours in total: a 30-minute research presentation, then a thirty-minute conversation, then an extra 15-minute one-to-one that was added at the end. The presentation could be any past project that could be shared without breaching confidentiality.
process.who: Presentation: Marcus Elling (the PM) and two researchers, Nadia and Felix. Then Ingrid Saarinen, head of research. Then Marcus alone.
process.what_they_look_for: Economic reasoning behind a signal (who is on the other side of the trade), robustness against standard factors, and a clear pre-agreed rule for when to cut or stop a signal. Ingrid's conversation covered culture, working style and how you deal with being wrong.

examples: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until a six
Expected number of coin flips until two heads in a row, and the heads-then-tails version
Three random points on a circle: probability the triangle contains the centre
A stick broken at two random points: probability the pieces form a triangle

question_themes.theme: Validating past research and avoiding overfitting
examples: How a momentum strategy handled crash periods such as 2009
Whether it was tested properly out of sample, and who chose the holdout
Whether a signal is just value in disguise and has been neutralised against standard factors
How many variants were tried, and deflating the Sharpe for the number of trials

question_themes.theme: Spotting flaws in backtests and data
examples: Look-ahead from trading at the same close used for the signal
Why series end part-way through (delistings, acquisitions) and survivorship bias
How to model market impact for small caps and what participation rate to assume

question_themes.theme: Signal economics and when to stop trading a signal
examples: Why the signal works economically and who is on the other side of the trade
What evidence or threshold would make you kill a signal live, and how long you would sit through a drawdown
Asked about notice and non-compete in the first round, second round and final round

went_well: In the first round, a candidate who first gave the wrong answer on two heads in a row caught it, corrected it and walked through the states. Graham said "good, you checked it".
In the second round, a candidate asked why series ended before computing anything and named survivorship bias. Nadia smiled at that.
In the second round, saying "I'd normally check the docs here" and writing pseudo-pandas was accepted, as Nadia said she cared about the logic.
In the second round, the candidate went through look-ahead, costs, turnover and multiple testing on the backtest.
In the final round, a backup slide showing the factor-neutral version of the signal answered Marcus's "value in disguise" challenge. The effect fell but remained, and Marcus said "OK, good".
In the final round, answering the kill question by cutting size rather than switching the signal off, and setting the rule before going live, got a lot of nodding from Felix.
tripped_people_up: On two heads in a row, one candidate first said four (the heads-then-tails answer) before correcting to six.
On the three points on a circle question, one candidate took a while and worked it out on paper, arriving at a quarter.
When asked who chose the holdout period in a momentum backtest, the candidate had to say it was them.
On market impact for small caps and participation rate, one candidate was hand-wavy.
In the second round, the exact pandas groupby syntax was not recalled without internet, so pseudo-code was used.
advice: Prepare for a first-round call with little feedback. Graham gave almost no reaction, so keep working through each problem and do not read his silence as a bad sign.
Practise classic expected-value and geometric probability questions, and say out loud how you check your answer. The coin-flip variants were used to test whether you understand why they differ.
Be ready to defend how you validated past work: out-of-sample design, who chose the holdout, behaviour in crashes, and neutralising against standard factors.
For the technical round, practise Python on messy price and volume data without internet. Ask why series stop, handle gaps and bad prints, and explain your logic as you go.
Prepare to critique a backtest in a structured way: look-ahead, costs and turnover, multiple testing, and a clear view on modelling market impact for small caps, including participation rates.

If you reach the final, prepare a presentation on a project you can share, with a backup slide on factor neutrality. Expect to be interrupted early, and have a view on why the signal works economically and what would make you cut or stop it.
Expect to be asked about notice and non-compete at each stage, and have the details of your own contract ready.
logistics: The first round was by video and the second and final rounds were at the firm's office.
The second round used a company laptop with no internet access.
In the second round, the start was late and the session lasted about two and a quarter hours.
The final round ran to about three hours including an extra 15-minute one-to-one with Marcus.
The final round presentation could be any past project that could be shared without breaching confidentiality.
Notice period and non-compete were asked about in the first round, the second round and the final round.

In the final round, Ingrid Saarinen said the firm does not buy out garden leave, as a matter of policy. She also said they are used to waiting and that it is not a deal-breaker, but asked whether the candidate would ask their current firm to shorten it.
In the final round, Marcus asked for references before an offer.
Your own record shows an 8-week notice period and a 3-month non-compete, so expect questions on both and be ready to say whether your current employer would shorten or pay through them.
Your next interview is booked for 27 November at 14:00.
